authoritative_sources.issuing_organization: Canadian Geriatrics Society Journal of CME
authoritative_sources.currentness_notes: Latest elder-abuse article in the Canadian Geriatrics Society journal collection found at retrieval; Volume 14, Issue 2 (2025) expressly describes the current shared federal and provincial/territorial legal context.

authoritative_sources.title: Medico-legal matters: Duty to report
authoritative_sources.currentness_notes: Current live CMPA Good Practices page checked on retrieval; it expressly requires physicians to consult the law and regulator rules of their own province or territory.

supported_recommendations.statement: When elder abuse or neglect is suspected, assess and document the older adult's immediate safety, decision-making capacity, wishes, relevant history and physical findings, and caregiver interactions; then determine whether reporting or limited disclosure is required or permitted under the law and regulator rules of the treating jurisdiction.

source_citations.locator: Key points; assessment, documentation, intervention, and provincial/territorial reporting-law discussion
Elder abuse in the Canadian context; shared jurisdiction and provincial/territorial variation
Duty to report; permission to warn; minimum-necessary disclosure and documentation

important_contraindications_or_exception.statement: There is no single Canada-wide mandatory-reporting rule for every elder-abuse presentation: duties and thresholds vary by province or territory and by setting, including legislation specific to persons in care or long-term care.

source_citations.locator: Elder abuse in the Canadian context
Duty to report: provincial and territorial nuances

important_contraindications_or_exception.statement: Where disclosure without consent is legally permitted to avert serious harm, disclose only the information sufficient for that protective purpose and document the disclosure and reasoning.

source_citations.locator: Permission to warn; sufficient-information and documentation guidance
Key points and approach
Elder abuse in the Canadian context
Duty to report and permission to warn

evidence_boundaries.statement: Do not treat age, dependency, a single warning sign, or suspected abuse as proof of incapacity; capacity and the reporting duty require case- and jurisdiction-specific assessment.

source_citations.locator: Assessment and intervention; capacity and provincial/territorial law discussion
Duty to report: threshold and clinical-assessment guidance

evidence_notes: The packet is limited to the legal and ethical physician response to suspected elder abuse; clinical recognition is included only insofar as it informs safety, capacity, documentation, confidentiality, and reporting.

authoritative_sources.guideline_version: Revised October 2023; current page includes October 2024 Quebec legal update
authoritative_sources.currentness_notes: CMPA marks the article revised October 2023; the live page contains the October 30, 2024 Quebec MAID advance-request update, confirming active maintenance.

authoritative_sources.title: Decision-Making for End-of-Life Care
authoritative_sources.issuing_organization: College of Physicians and Surgeons of Ontario
authoritative_sources.currentness_notes: Current CPSO policy checked on retrieval; the policy page identifies March 2023 as its latest completed review and update.

guideline_versions: Revised October 2023; current page includes October 2024 Quebec legal update

supported_recommendations.statement: Advance care planning should identify and communicate a capable patient's values, wishes, and substitute decision-maker for future incapacity, but it does not replace consent for a specific treatment. When significant illness creates foreseeable decisions, conduct a timely goals-of-care discussion covering diagnosis, prognosis, available treatments including resuscitation, realistic outcomes, and the patient's values, then revisit the discussion when circumstances change.

source_citations.locator: Advance care planning; ACP is not a replacement for consent; ACP versus advance directive
Definitions; policy provisions 1-3, Advance Care Planning and Goals of Care Discussions

important_contraindications_or_exception.statement: An advance care plan is not itself contemporaneous consent, and the identity, authority, and decision rules for substitute decision-makers or advance directives depend on provincial or territorial law.

source_citations.locator: ACP is not a replacement for consent; ACP versus advance directive

important_contraindications_or_exception.statement: Ontario's current policy distinguishes withdrawing life-sustaining treatment, which requires patient or substitute-decision-maker consent, from writing an order to withhold resuscitative measures when CPR is outside the standard of care; this Ontario rule must not be generalized without checking the treating jurisdiction.

source_citations.locator: Policy provisions 4-10; endnotes citing Rasouli and Wawrzyniak
Advance care planning and consent sections
Advance Care Planning and Goals of Care Discussions; End-of-Life Care

evidence_boundaries.statement: A no-CPR or DNR order addresses resuscitation after cardiopulmonary arrest; it does not mean withholding other clinically appropriate treatment or palliative care.

source_citations.locator: Withholding Resuscitative Measures; Providing Support if Disagreements Arise

evidence_notes: National CMPA guidance establishes the cross-Canada consent boundary; Ontario regulator policy supplies a concrete provincial implementation without being represented as a uniform Canadian rule.

source_family_target_assessments.rationale: The packet is legal and ethical rather than therapeutic. Current national CMPA medico-legal guidance directly governs the ACP-versus-consent distinction and jurisdictional variation, so it is a more authoritative fit than a specialty-society clinical document.

authoritative_sources.title: The Canadian Interdisciplinary Palliative Care Competency Framework
authoritative_sources.issuing_organization: Canadian Partnership Against Cancer and Health Canada
authoritative_sources.currentness_notes: Health Canada's current professional palliative-care resource page continues to link this framework. The document establishes a national minimum standard and states that provincial or territorial adaptations may be required.

authoritative_sources.title: Decision-Making for End-of-Life Care
authoritative_sources.issuing_organization: College of Physicians and Surgeons of Ontario
authoritative_sources.currentness_notes: Current CPSO policy checked on retrieval; the policy page identifies March 2023 as its latest completed review and update.

supported_recommendations.statement: Provide palliative care through person- and family-centred interdisciplinary collaboration: clarify team roles, communicate continuously, coordinate referrals and transitions, and develop and revise the care plan with the patient and designated family or caregiver so it remains aligned with goals of care, preferences, and any advance care plan.

source_citations.locator: Generalist Physicians competencies: Principles of a palliative approach to care; Care planning and collaborative practice
Managing Disagreements and Providing Support if Disagreements Arise

important_contraindications_or_exception.statement: Team composition and professional roles vary with the patient's changing needs, available resources, regulated scopes of practice, and province or territory; collaboration does not make every listed discipline mandatory in every case.

source_citations.locator: Introduction: provincial and territorial adaptation; interdisciplinary-team and collaborative-practice competencies

important_contraindications_or_exception.statement: Support from the interdisciplinary team does not displace the capable patient's treatment authority or the legally authorized substitute decision-maker's role when the patient is incapable.

source_citations.locator: Advance Care Planning and Goals of Care Discussions; Withdrawing Life-Sustaining Treatment
Generalist Physicians competencies, domains 1 and 5
End-of-life decision-making and supportive-services provisions

evidence_boundaries.statement: Interprofessional consensus is not a substitute for consent: the team informs, coordinates, and supports decision-making while the patient or legally authorized substitute decision-maker provides or refuses consent under applicable law.

source_citations.locator: Care planning and collaborative practice
Withdrawing Life-Sustaining Treatment; Managing Disagreements

evidence_notes: This packet is restricted to the ethical and role-boundary aspects of interdisciplinary palliative collaboration; symptom-specific treatment is outside scope.

source_family_target_assessments.rationale: The joint Health Canada and Canadian Partnership Against Cancer framework establishes the pan-Canadian minimum interdisciplinary competency standard, was developed with the Canadian Society of Palliative Care Physicians, and is the current higher-authority national source for this collaboration requirement.

authoritative_sources.issuing_organization: College of Physicians and Surgeons of Ontario

authoritative_sources.title: Consent: A guide for Canadian physicians
authoritative_sources.currentness_notes: CMPA identifies this as the fourth edition revised October 2024; the current text expressly incorporates Quebec's October 30, 2024 MAID advance-request regime.

supported_recommendations.statement: Respond to a MAID request without assuming eligibility: clarify that it is a voluntary patient request, assess decision-making capacity and freedom from external pressure, provide the information needed for informed consent including diagnosis, treatments and available means to relieve suffering such as palliative care, and connect the patient with the applicable provincial or territorial assessment pathway.

source_citations.locator: Curriculum topics: Clinical Conversations that Include MAiD; How to do a MAiD assessment; Assessing Capacity and Vulnerability
Eligibility; Informed consent; Making a request; Role of provinces and territories
MAID Providers and Assessors; capacity, grievous-and-irremediable-condition, and request/reporting guidance

supported_recommendations.statement: Federal eligibility does not require a terminal condition, but every criterion must be met and two independent practitioners must confirm eligibility. When natural death is not reasonably foreseeable, the additional Track 2 safeguards include relevant-condition expertise or consultation, discussion of reasonable available means to relieve suffering, and a minimum 90-day assessment period unless assessments are complete and loss of capacity is imminent.

source_citations.locator: Eligibility; Procedural safeguards; Requests where natural death is not reasonably foreseeable
Grievous and irremediable medical condition; 90-day assessment period

important_contraindications_or_exception.statement: A person whose sole underlying medical condition is a mental illness is not eligible for MAID before March 17, 2027; a person with mental illness plus another qualifying condition may still be individually assessed under the current criteria.

source_citations.locator: Eligibility: mental illness exclusion
Grievous and irremediable medical condition

important_contraindications_or_exception.statement: A waiver of final consent is not a general advance request: federally it is available only after eligibility is established and, for clinician-administered MAID, when natural death is reasonably foreseeable and the statutory written arrangement is completed. Quebec separately permits advance requests under its provincial law as of October 30, 2024, creating a jurisdiction-specific situation requiring current local guidance.

source_citations.locator: Final consent; waiver of final consent
Waivers of Final Consent
Mental incapacity and substitute decision-making: Quebec advance requests and waiver of final consent

important_contraindications_or_exception.statement: A substitute decision-maker cannot request or consent to MAID on behalf of an incapable patient under the general Canadian framework.

source_citations.locator: Mental incapacity and substitute decision-making
Curriculum overview and eight topic areas
Eligibility, consent, and procedural safeguards
MAID assessment and waiver guidance
Consent forms and medical assistance in dying; Quebec jurisdictional exception

evidence_boundaries.statement: A request or inquiry initiates respectful information-giving and pathway access; it does not establish eligibility, and a request cannot be accepted from a substitute decision-maker on the patient's behalf.

source_citations.locator: Making a request; Medical assessments
Mental incapacity and substitute decision-making

evidence_boundaries.statement: Reasonable foreseeability of natural death determines which safeguard track applies; it is not itself a universal eligibility requirement for MAID.
